inputs.need:
I am a neurologist running the adult epilepsy clinic at a university hospital, together with two epilepsy nurse specialists. Two years ago we started recommending a free self-management app to our patients: it has a seizure diary, medication reminders, trigger tracking and a report that patients can show us at clinic. About 40 percent of our 1,100 patients say they downloaded it, but when we ask at clinic, most stopped using it within a few weeks, and the reports we see are mostly empty.

Before we invest nurse time in coaching patients to use the app, or ask the hospital to build its own, we want to understand what is known about engagement with epilepsy self-management apps. I have in mind a scoping review: how engagement has been defined and measured, what levels of engagement have been reported and for how long, which features and which kinds of support go with sustained use, whether engagement has been linked to outcomes such as medication adherence, seizure recording or quality of life, and who tends not to engage at all (older adults, people with intellectual disability, people without smartphones or data plans).

We have no funding beyond clinic time. One of the nurse specialists and a neurology resident can screen, and the neurosciences library can help with searches. We want results by June 2027 to inform a clinic decision. No patient data can leave the hospital, and this review will not involve our patients directly.
inputs.constraints: No funding beyond clinic time. Screening by one epilepsy nurse specialist and one neurology resident, about three hours a week each. Results needed by June 2027. No patient data may leave the hospital, and the review will not involve clinic patients.

About 1,100 adults attend the epilepsy clinic; about 40 percent report having downloaded the recommended app.
The clinic's decision on nurse coaching or a hospital-built app is scheduled for July 2027.

records.title: Engagement with a smartphone seizure diary and self-reported seizure control: a 12-month observational study
records.authors: Mahlaba-Frost E, Kuznetsov-Adeyemi R, Lindgren-Obi T
records.abstract: We followed 486 adults with epilepsy who installed a seizure diary app recommended by their clinic. Engagement was defined as at least one diary entry per week. At one month, 61 percent were engaged; at six months, 23 percent; at twelve months, 14 percent. Sustained users reported fewer missed doses, but they were also older, more often employed and had fewer seizures at baseline. Diary entries matched clinic-recorded seizures for 70 percent of sustained users. The authors caution that engagement and seizure control may share causes rather than one driving the other.

records.title: How engagement is measured in self-management apps for chronic neurological conditions: a methodological review
records.abstract: We reviewed 61 studies of self-management apps for epilepsy, multiple sclerosis, migraine and Parkinson disease to see how engagement was defined. We found 23 different engagement measures. Log-ins and days of use were the most common, used in 38 studies; only 9 studies measured use of specific features, and 5 used a validated self-report engagement scale. Nineteen studies did not define engagement at all. Follow-up for engagement rarely exceeded three months. The authors propose reporting both use of core features and duration of use.

records.title: Medication reminder use and antiseizure medication adherence measured by electronic pill boxes
records.authors: Carvalho-Nyambura J, Stewart-Ikeda M, Brenner-Oduya K
records.abstract: We compared app reminder logs with electronic pill box openings for 142 adults taking antiseizure medication over 90 days. Participants who acknowledged at least 80 percent of reminders had pill box adherence of 92 percent, compared with 78 percent for those who acknowledged fewer. Reminder use declined steadily over the 90 days. Participants who set their own reminder times acknowledged more reminders than those who used default times. The study did not measure seizures or quality of life, and participants were volunteers from one clinic.

records.title: Why adults with epilepsy stop using self-management apps: a thematic analysis of 30 accounts
records.abstract: We analysed written and spoken accounts from 30 adults with epilepsy who had stopped using a self-management app. Reasons included the effort of daily entries, apps that did not fit irregular seizure patterns, worry about who could see the data, and a lack of response from clinicians to the reports. Several participants said they would have kept using the app if a nurse had looked at their entries at clinic. People with memory problems after seizures found reminders helpful but diaries hard to complete.

records.title: Digital access and app uptake among people with epilepsy in rural and low-income areas
records.authors: Quispe-Harrington L, Bakshi-Wolde D, Thornton-Achebe M
records.abstract: Among 1,020 adults attending four epilepsy clinics, 81 percent owned a smartphone, but ownership was 58 percent among those aged over 65 and 64 percent among those in the lowest income quintile. Of smartphone owners offered a self-management app, 47 percent installed it; installation was lower among people with intellectual disability and people who shared a phone. Limited mobile data was the reason most often given for not installing. The authors recommend that engagement studies report who was offered an app, not only who used it.

records.title: Retention curves for health apps: an analysis of 1.2 million installs
records.abstract: Using anonymous usage data from 1.2 million installs of 94 health apps, we estimated retention over 90 days. Seventy percent of users stopped opening an app within 30 days, and 88 percent within 90 days. Apps with reminders and clinician-linked features retained users longer, but retention also varied with the condition and the age of users. Usage data could not show whether people who stopped had benefited. The analysis did not include apps for epilepsy specifically, and app developers chose which data to share.

records.title: Self-management programmes for epilepsy delivered digitally: a review of trials
records.abstract: We identified nine trials of digitally delivered self-management programmes for adults with epilepsy, with 1,340 participants. Programmes improved self-management scores modestly at three to six months. No trial showed a difference in seizure frequency, and only two reported engagement in enough detail to relate it to outcomes. Most trials excluded people with intellectual disability, and none reported outcomes by age or income. Follow-up beyond six months was reported by one trial only. The authors conclude that engagement is the missing link between digital programmes and outcomes.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Engagement with epilepsy self-management apps falls steeply over months, is measured in many incompatible ways, and has not been linked to seizure outcomes in trials. People stop for reasons of effort, fit, privacy and the absence of clinician response, and many older or low-income people lack a smartphone in the first place. Reminder use goes with better adherence in one small study. The field is fragmented and definitional, which suits mapping rather than pooling.
response.gradeRationale: Observational and qualitative studies and one trial review with inconsistent engagement definitions; low certainty for any link between engagement and outcomes.
response.summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; four claims with passages; certainty low.

steps.note: Applied through the appraisal mapper on the production scan path (S13); certainty over seven inspected records (G1).

response.reading: Engagement is shaped before, during and after install: access to a device and data (claim c4), the effort and fit of the app, and whether anyone at clinic looks at the entries (claim c3). Measures of engagement are inconsistent (claim c2) and engagement decays within months (claim c1), so any claim that engagement improves outcomes rests on thin ground. The clinic's choice between coaching and building an app depends on which of these links the literature describes.

response.title: Engagement with self-management apps among adults with epilepsy: a scoping review
response.abstract: Objective: to map how engagement with epilepsy self-management apps is defined, measured and sustained, which features and clinician support accompany sustained use, which outcomes are reported alongside engagement, and who does not engage. Design: scoping review following JBI guidance, reported with PRISMA-ScR. Results will be charted by June 2027.
response.introduction: Clinics recommend self-management apps, but engagement decays within months, is measured inconsistently and has not been linked to seizure outcomes in trials.
response.methods: Searches of four databases, two app-evaluation repositories and charity websites by the library; dual screening; charting verified by a second reviewer; outcomes charted as associations.
response.results: No charting has been done yet. The report will present the PRISMA-ScR flow diagram and maps of definitions, engagement over time, features and support, outcomes and access.
response.discussion: The discussion will state what the map means for choosing between nurse coaching and a hospital-built app.
response.limitations: English only; incompatible engagement definitions; favourable commercial reports.
response.conclusion: To be written after charting; it will describe the field and not estimate effects.
response.summary: PRISMA-ScR draft with results left empty until charting.
